full_judgment: 7. In this respect it may be mentioned that after pronouncement of judgment in the case of Tarkeswar Prasnd Tewari vs Devendra Prasad Tewari which was considered in PLD 1967 (Lah) 1951 a full Bench of Madras High Court had an occasion to deal with this question in the case of Katikineni Venkata Gopal Naras-simha vs Chitluri Venkataramayya reported in 1940 (Mad) 768 wherein it has been held that both plaint bad written statement are public documents. I have gone through the decision reported in PLD 1967 (Lah) 1051 as well as 19 DLR 349. I prefer to follow the view taken by his Lordship Abdullah, J which I consider to be a correct exposition on the interpretation of section 74 of the Evidence Act. The plaint of a suit, in my opinion, as soon as it is registered by the Court on presentation it forms part of the record of the judicial officer within the meaning of clause (in) of sub-section (1) of section 74 of the Evidence Act and as soon as it forms part of the records of judicial officer it becomes admissible in evidence. In this view of the matter, with the reference to the learned judge who decided the case reported in PLD 1967 (Lah) 1057 I am unable to follow the view taken by him. Therefore the contention of the learned Advocate that the finding of the Lower Appellate Court is based on inadmissible evidence viz the certified copy of plaint of TS No. 201 of 1956 cannot be upheld. The learned Advocate for the petitioners also submitted that the finding of the lower appellate court regarding 'Estafa' by the tenant Rahimuddin, Reazuddin and Gaizuddin in favour of the superior landlords was also not based on proper consideration of evidence as the learned Appellate Court did not advert to the reasoning of the trial court and consider evidence relied on by it. The learned Advocate for the opposite, parties, on the other bands, submitted that in this case although the Lower Appellate Court did not consider all the documents on record which were considered by the trial court yet the finding being based on sufficient evidence cannot be interfered with by this court. I was taken through the judgments of the both courts, From the judgment of the lower appellate court it appears that it took into consideration the averments made in the plaint of Title Suit No. 201 of 1956, miscellaneous proceeding case No 562 of 1970 and Money Suit No. 6 of 1969 for the purpose of holding that the surrender was not acted upon. The finding as to whether a document by which certain land was surrendered was acted upon or not has to be arrived at with reference to the evidence on record. Although the lower Appellate Court did not take into consideration each and every piece of document considered by trial Court in arriving at the finding regarding surrender of the land by Rahimuddin, Reazuddin and Gaisuddin but then the Low Appellate Court on consideration of the certified copy of the plaint, Miscellaneous proceeding case and the Money Suit found that the deed of surrender was not acted upon. In this respect it is pertinent to observe that the Lower Appellate Court for arriving at a conclusion of its own on facts need not refer to each, and every piece of document considered by the trial court if the evidence relied upon by it for such conclusion are sufficient for arriving at such a finding either of reversal or affirmance. In this case learned Lower Appellate Court having based his finding on consideration of the aforesaid documents and evidence on record I do not think that the finding is liable to be set-aside.
